reference.source: Green's Operative Hand Surgery / Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: Presents as loss of active extension at the distal interphalangeal joint with a characteristic dropped, flexed fingertip
Typically caused by sudden forced flexion of an actively extended fingertip, such as a ball striking the end of the digit
The injury may be purely tendinous (soft-tissue avulsion of the terminal extensor tendon) or bony (a dorsal avulsion fracture of the distal phalanx base)
A large bony fragment associated with volar subluxation of the distal phalanx renders the joint unstable and warrants surgical assessment
A chronic untreated mallet can lead to a secondary swan-neck deformity as extensor force is transmitted proximally to hyperextend the proximal interphalangeal joint
Lateral radiographs are essential to define the size of any fragment and confirm joint congruity
Generic management is continuous extension splinting of the distal interphalangeal joint for several weeks in most closed injuries, with the proximal interphalangeal joint left free
Surgery is reserved for a large displaced fragment, joint subluxation or an open injury
reference.pathophysiology: A mallet finger arises from disruption of the terminal extensor tendon at its insertion on the dorsal base of the distal phalanx, either through a tendinous avulsion or through a dorsal avulsion fracture. Loss of active extensor input leaves the flexor digitorum profundus unopposed, so the distal phalanx rests in flexion. Over time the disrupted balance of the extensor mechanism can shift force proximally through the central slip and lateral bands, hyperextending the proximal interphalangeal joint and producing a secondary swan-neck posture.
additionalDifferentials: Distal phalanx or distal interphalangeal joint fracture-dislocation
Flexor digitorum profundus avulsion (jersey finger), which causes the opposite deficit
Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis of the distal interphalangeal joint
Distal interphalangeal osteoarthritis with a mallet-like posture
A more proximal extensor mechanism or sagittal band injury
Open laceration of the terminal tendon
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment documenting the extension lag at the distal interphalangeal joint
Lateral plain radiograph to identify a bony mallet, quantify fragment size and detect volar subluxation
Assessment of overall joint congruity and stability
Examination of the overlying skin to exclude an open injury or skin loss
Ultrasound occasionally to evaluate the terminal tendon when imaging is equivocal
redFlags: Volar subluxation of the distal phalanx indicating an unstable joint
An open injury or threatened skin necrosis beneath the splint
An established fixed deformity or secondary swan-neck
reference.prognosis: Outcomes are generally good with early continuous splinting; delayed presentation or interrupted splinting commonly leaves a small residual extension lag that is usually well tolerated functionally.
pitfalls: Inadequate or interrupted splinting, since allowing the joint to flex even briefly resets the healing process
Skin maceration or pressure necrosis from an ill-fitting or overtightened splint
Missing volar subluxation that requires surgical rather than splint treatment
Overlooking the development of a secondary swan-neck deformity
management: Continuous splinting of the distal interphalangeal joint in extension for an uninterrupted period, leaving the proximal interphalangeal joint free, for closed tendinous and most bony injuries
Emphasise uninterrupted splint wear, since any episode of flexion during healing restarts the process, supported by hand therapy education
Surgical fixation, such as with a Kirschner wire, for a large avulsion fragment with volar subluxation, an unstable joint or an open injury
Wound care and soft-tissue cover for open injuries with skin loss
Graduated mobilisation and splint weaning under hand therapy guidance after the immobilisation period
For chronic deformity or secondary swan-neck, consider surgical reconstruction or arthrodesis
Refer to hand surgery when the joint is unstable, the fragment large, or presentation is delayed
